questions.question_text: A 30-year-old male, a patient with antisocial personality traits, has been admitted to the inpatient psychiatric ward. The nurses are now complaining much about the difficulties with managing him. They are angry with him and want him to be transferred. Which of the following psychological process is occurring?
questions.explanation: This is commonly referred to as the therapist’s own feelings, emotions and attitudes towards his or her patient.

questions.question_text: Based on epidemiological studies in the United Kingdom, which of the following is known to be the most common methodology of committing suicide?
questions.explanation: It is essential to note that psychiatric patients tend to use violent methods such as hanging, shooting and jumping from heights. For the general population, two thirds of the British men and one third of the British women commit suicide by hanging or via inhalation of vehicular exhaust fumes. Drowning is the most common amongst older people.

questions.question_text: In which of the following inherited genetic conditions would dietary restriction and close monitoring of dietary habits be of use in terms of management?
questions.explanation: The commonest presentation for the disorder would be that of irresistible hunger drive and also excessive skin picking with associated compulsion and anxiety. Given that insatiable appetite is a core diagnostic feature, dietary restriction should be used as it would help to reduce obesity.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old male has tried two antipsychotic medications, but both of them did not help him with his symptoms. The team has recommended and started him on clozapine, with which he has not experienced much improvement still. He is currently on clozapine 400 mg ON. Based on the guidelines, which one of the following could be used to help him with his symptoms?

options.text: Continue clozapine treatment but titrate the medication to 1000 mg/day, as he is treatment resistant.
Continue clozapine treatment but titrate the medication to a maximum of 900 mg/day, as he is treatment resistant.
Consider adding lithium to augment the effects of the drug.
Consider adding omega-3 fatty acids to enhance the effectiveness of clozapine.

correct_answer.text: Continue clozapine treatment but titrate the medication to a maximum of 900 mg/day, as he is treatment resistant.

correct_answers.text: Continue clozapine treatment but titrate the medication to a maximum of 900 mg/day, as he is treatment resistant.

questions.explanation: Clozapine is indicated usually for patients with schizophrenia that is not well controlled despite the sequential usage of two or more of the antipsychotics, of which one should be atypical, and the medication should have been used for the past 6–8 weeks. The average dose in the UK is around 450 mg/day. Response could be seen in the range 150–900 mg/day. Commencement of an intramuscular depot, addition of lithium and addition of Omega 3 fatty acids are unlikely to be helpful in his condition.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old male was admitted to the emergency department following a collapse at the shopping mall. A routine CT brain was performed, and the radiologist reported marked atrophy of the caudate nucleus. Which of the following clinical diagnoses would be the most appropriate?
questions.explanation: This is defined as a genetic disorder that has the following features: continuous involuntary movements and a slowly progressive dementia. CT scan might show a reduction in the volume of the caudate nucleus.

questions.question_text: Based on your understanding about psychotherapy, which of the following statements about interpersonal therapy is incorrect?

options.text: It is focused much on the earlier childhood events that the client has undergone.
It involves dealing with role transition.
It involves dealing with deficits in interpersonal relationships.

correct_answer.text: It is focused much on the earlier childhood events that the client has undergone.

correct_answers.text: It is focused much on the earlier childhood events that the client has undergone.

questions.explanation: Interpersonal therapy deals with the following areas: grief, interpersonal disputes, role transitions and interpersonal role deficits. The main objective is to create a therapeutic environment with meaningful therapeutic relationship and the ability to recognize the client’s underlying attachment needs.

questions.question_text: A medical student wonders which of the following anxiety disorders would have the earliest age of onset. The correct answer would be
questions.explanation: Social phobia would have the earliest age of onset. Based on epidemiological studies, generalized anxiety disorder would first occur in the 20s; panic disorder at the age of 15–24 years and social phobia usually at the ages of 11–15 years.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the aetiology of autism is incorrect?

options.text: The heritability of autism is around 50%.
The male to female ratio is around 4:1.
Genetic causative factors might include a positive family history of schizophrenia like psychosis or affective disorder.
Maternal use of sodium valproate might cause autism.
Perinatal injuries and antenatal infections are aetiological factors that are responsible for the development of autism.

correct_answer.text: The heritability of autism is around 50%.

correct_answers.text: The heritability of autism is around 50%.

questions.explanation: The heritability of autism is around 90% instead of 50%. The male-to-female ratio is estimated to be 4:1. Autism accounts for around 25%–60% of all autistic disorders. There have not been studies demonstrating an association between autistic disorder and any socioeconomic status. The recurrent rate in siblings is roughly 3% for narrowly defined autism but is about 10%–20% for milder variants. Perinatal injuries (such as maternal bleeding after the first trimester or meconium in the amniotic fluid) or antenatal infections or the use of sodium valproate in pregnancy might result in the development of autism.

questions.question_text: It is known that some genetic disorders are caused by mutations that have occurred in the body cells and are inherited to the next generation. Which particular type of genetic mutation would not have an impact on the next generation?
questions.explanation: A somatic mutation occurs after fertilization and is only present in a subpopulation of somatic cells. This differs from a germline mutation, which refers to a mutation that originates from a gamete that is then fused with another gamete during fertilization, thus leading to conception of an individual who has mutation in every cell.

questions.question_text: In order for the transcribed RNA to be processed for translation, which of the following must happen first?

options.text: The introns must be separated first.
There must be methylation happening to the start end of the transcribed RNA.
There must be methylation happening to the tail end of the transcribed RNA.
There must be the splicing of the cap of the transcribed RNA.
There must be splicing and methylation of the cap of the transcribed RNA.

correct_answer.text: The introns must be separated first.

correct_answers.text: The introns must be separated first.

questions.explanation: Once transcription has taken place, it is followed by splicing and nuclear transport, so that the information (minus that from the introns) then exists in the cytoplasm of the cell on messenger RNA. The splicing out of the introns is guided by the recognition of the GT and AG dinucleotides that mark the beginning and the end of the intron.

questions.question_text: Which of the following therapies would be the most effective for a patient with obsessive-compulsive disorder, whose main fears are that of contamination and compulsions are that of repeated washing?
questions.explanation: Based on the NICE guidelines, for the initial treatment of OCD, exposure and response prevention (up to 10 therapist hours per client) should be offered. For adults with mild-to-moderate functional impairment, more intensive CBT (including ERP) (more than 10 therapist hours per client) would be recommended.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old female just had a recent first episode of schizophrenia and she has been concordant with her medications since discharge. Her mother is worried about the long-term side effects of the medication and wanted to know for how long pharmacological treatment should be continued. The correct answer would be
questions.explanation: In the maintenance phase of schizophrenia, antipsychotic drugs should be continued for at least 1 or 2 years after the last acute episode. It is still important to continue to monitor for adverse effects related to the treatment. Withdrawal of antipsychotic medication should be gradual and monitored. Following the withdrawal of drugs, patients should be monitored for the signs of relapse for at least 2 years after the last acute episode.

questions.question_text: In which of the following conditions would there be the presence of eosinophilic inclusion with high amyloid content in the cingulated gyrus?
questions.explanation: Lewy bodies are commonly located in the cingulated gyrus, the cortex and the substantial nigra. They contain eosinophilic inclusion with high amyloid content, but with the absence of tau pathology. Lewy bodies are alpha-synuclein and ubiquitin positive. Alpha-synuclein is an aggregated and insoluble protein, which is pathognomonic of Lewy body dementia and idiopathic Parkinson’s disease.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old male would like to have some help with regards to his alcohol addiction issues. He has read about ‘disulfiram’ and is wondering how this medication can help him. What is the mechanism of action of the drug?

options.text: It is an aversive agent which inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), thus leading to acetaldehyde accumulation after drinking alcohol.
It works as a GABA agonist and glutamate antagonist.
It inactivates the N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptors and helps to prevent calcium influx.

correct_answer.text: It is an aversive agent which inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), thus leading to acetaldehyde accumulation after drinking alcohol.

correct_answers.text: It is an aversive agent which inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), thus leading to acetaldehyde accumulation after drinking alcohol.

questions.explanation: The medication works as an aversive agent, and the doctor who prescribes has to make sure that the patient has not consumed alcohol over the past 1 day prior to commencement. It would inhibit ALDH2 and this would lead to an accumulation of acetaldehyde, which would result in unpleasant side effects on consumption of alcohol. Aversive effects include flushing, headache, palpitations, tachycardia, nausea and vomiting with ingestion of small amounts of alcohol, and air hunger, arrhythmias and severe hypotension with large amounts of alcohol. These effects occur 10–30 minutes after drinking and are dose dependent. The reaction to alcohol discourages the person from drinking and reduces the number of days spent on drinking.

questions.question_text: For a patient with OCD, whose main obsessions are that of fears of contamination and main compulsions are that of repeated washing, which of the following correctly describes how exposure and response prevention would help?

options.text: Therapist telling the patient to keep using deep breathing when she is anxious
Therapist challenging the automatic thoughts of the patient
Therapist telling the patient to intentionally touch something contaminated, but preventing her from doing her usual compulsion
Therapist gradually limiting the number of times the patient is allowed to perform the compulsion
Therapist advising the patient to consider other forms of distractions when she is compelled to perform her compulsions

correct_answer.text: Therapist telling the patient to intentionally touch something contaminated, but preventing her from doing her usual compulsion

correct_answers.text: Therapist telling the patient to intentionally touch something contaminated, but preventing her from doing her usual compulsion

questions.explanation: In this example, in order to prevent the response of excessive washing, the therapist should tell the patient to intentionally touch something contaminated, but prevent her from doing her usual compulsions.

questions.question_text: Genetic studies have identified that trinucleotide repeat expansions are responsible for the following genetic disorder:
questions.explanation: The clinical features of the fragile X syndrome are due to the failure of the FMR1 gene transcription due to hyper-methylation, thus resulting in the absence of the FMR1 gene protein. Normal number of repeats is 30, and the repeats for carriers range from 55 to 2000. Full mutation with more than 200 repeats leads to hyper-methylation at the gene.

questions.question_text: A 27-year-old female has bipolar disorder and is currently on treatment. She presented to the emergency department with the following symptoms: nausea, diarrhoea and coarse tremors. She claimed that she has just seen her GP last week and has just been started on some painkillers for her lower back pain. Which of the following is the likely cause of her current symptoms?
questions.explanation: The presentation is very likely lithium toxicity. It is important to note that the therapeutic index of lithium is low, and therefore regular lithium level monitoring would be required. At a toxic dose of above 2 mM, the following effects could occur: hyper-reflexia, hyperextension of all the limbs, toxic psychosis, convulsions, syncope, oliguria, circulatory failure, coma and death.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male suffered from a stroke around a year ago. His wife has noticed that his memory has been deteriorating and he is currently no longer able to manage himself. An MMSE was conducted during the out-patient visit, but he was also referred to a psychologist for an evaluation of his cognitive abilities prior to the onset of the stroke. Which toolkit would be the most helpful in this case?
questions.explanation: The National Adult Reading Test is a reading test consisting of phonetically irregular words that have to be read aloud by the subject. If a patient suffers deterioration in intellectual abilities, their premorbid vocabulary may remain less affected or even unaffected. The NART thus could be used to estimate the premorbid IQ.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old female has been referred to the mental health service, as she has been increasingly paranoid. After ruling out medical conditions, she has been diagnosed with late-onset schizophrenia. Which of the following statements about late-onset schizophrenia is true?

options.text: Most of those with late-onset schizophrenia are females.
Most of those with late-onset schizophrenia are males.
The treatment for late-onset schizophrenia is different from the treatment of early-onset schizophrenia.
Late-onset schizophrenia is not mediated by genetic factors.
Sensory impairment has not been associated with the development of paraphrenia.

correct_answer.text: Most of those with late-onset schizophrenia are females.

correct_answers.text: Most of those with late-onset schizophrenia are females.

questions.explanation: It has been established that late-onset schizophrenia is actually more prevalent in females. Individuals with late-onset psychosis are likely to be unmarried and have a lower reproductive rate as compared to controls. Late-onset schizophrenia is partly genetically determined, but the part played by inheritance requires further investigation and research. In a subset of patients, there is a history of those who have long-standing paranoid personalities, which are thought to predispose to the development of the disorder in the old age. Hearing impairment and sensory impairment have been associated with the development of paranoid symptoms.

questions.question_text: Which of the following chromosomal types is characterized by the central location of a centromere?
questions.explanation: Metacentric chromosome refers to a chromosome with a centrally or almost centrally positioned centromere. This should be distinguished from an acrocentric chromosome, in which the centromere is very near to one end.

questions.question_text: During a routine outpatient review, the core trainee noted that the patient whom he is seeing has tardive dyskinesia. Which of the following treatments would help with the symptoms?

options.text: Increasing the dose of the antipsychotics
Reducing the dose of the antipsychotics

correct_answer.text: Reducing the dose of the antipsychotics

correct_answers.text: Reducing the dose of the antipsychotics

questions.explanation: Tardive dyskinesia refers to a wide variety of movements that can occur, such as lip smacking or chewing, tongue protrusion, choreiform hand movements and pelvic thrusting. The severe movements involving the facial muscles can lead to difficulty with speaking, eating or breathing. Movements are usually worst under stress. They tend to be more common in elderly women and those with affective illness. In order to reduce the side effects, any anticholinergic should be stopped. The existing dose of the antipsychotic could be reduced, or if on a typical antipsychotic, changed to an atypical. Clozapine has been shown most likely to resolve these symptoms.

questions.question_text: Following a cerebrovascular accident, a 35-year-old male finds that he is unable to read, but when words are spelt out by his wife, he is able to recognize the words immediately. This is most commonly due to a lesion involving which one of the following arteries?
questions.explanation: Occlusion of the left posterior cerebral artery can infarct the medial aspect of the left occipital lobe and the splenium of the corpus callosum. The lesion in the splenium prevents transfer of visual information from the right to the left hemisphere, disconnecting the primary language area from written input (pure alexia). Although he cannot read printed words, he can recognize them when spelled out orally.

questions.question_text: As compared to normal individuals, patients who are diagnosed with schizophrenia are more likely to have an increased mortality rate. This rate has been established to be around
questions.explanation: Epidemiological studies show that schizophrenia carries at least a two- to three-fold increased mortality compared with the general population, due mainly to suicide and medical comorbidities. Life expectancy is approximately 10 years shorter.

questions.question_text: The dermatologist has referred a patient with schizophrenia to see the psychiatrist, as the patient has been having long-standing paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations. Which of the following antipsychotics would be contraindicated if the patient has a dermatological condition that is photosensitive?
questions.explanation: Chlorpromazine is associated with photosensitization, hypothermia or pyrexia, allergic skin reactions and can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome in susceptible patients. Other antipsychotics are less likely to cause clinically significant phototoxic reactions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is one of the metabolites of serotonin?
questions.explanation: 5-Hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) is the principal metabolite of serotonin. Its concentration in the CSF correlates with central serotonin turnover. Low CSF 5-HIAA is associated with violent behaviour and treatment-resistant depression.

questions.question_text: Based on previous genetic studies, which of the following statements about autosomal recessive transmission is true?

options.text: Individuals who marry their siblings are at a high risk.

correct_answer.text: Individuals who marry their siblings are at a high risk.

correct_answers.text: Individuals who marry their siblings are at a high risk.

questions.explanation: Rarer autosomal recessive disorders are more common in consanguineous unions. Heterozygous carriers are usually asymptomatic. The trait tends to appear in siblings (horizontal transmission), with a 25% risk in each pregnancy when both parents are carriers.

questions.question_text: Studies have shown that there has been an association between deficits in smooth eye pursuit tracking and which of the following psychiatric disorders?
questions.explanation: Smooth pursuit eye‐tracking deficits are robustly replicated in schizophrenia. They reflect underlying disturbances in neural systems mediating the coordination of eye movements and predictive tracking.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the main artery that supplies Broca’s area?
questions.explanation: Broca’s area (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) lies in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere and is supplied by the superior division of the middle cerebral artery.

questions.question_text: A 32-year-old female has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder since she was 20. She is now planning to start a family. She is concerned about the risk of foetal malformations as she has been on sodium valproate. The risk associated with the use of sodium valproate in pregnancy has been estimated to be
questions.explanation: Sodium valproate is one of the most teratogenic mood stabilizers. The risk of major congenital malformations is approximately 1% when used in pregnancy, and current guidelines recommend avoiding its use if possible.

questions.question_text: A neurologist is seeing a patient who has presented to his clinic with sudden onset of coarse and hoarse voice. In addition, he has been having swallowing difficulties. Injury to which of the following cranial nerves should be suspected?
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) supplies motor fibres to the palate, pharynx, larynx and upper oesophagus, and sensory fibres from the same areas plus parasympathetic fibres to thoracic and abdominal viscera. Injury leads to hoarseness, dysphagia and palatal weakness.

questions.question_text: Based on epidemiology studies, which of the following is the second most common cause of dementia?
questions.explanation: Vascular dementia is the second most common cause of dementia after Alzheimer’s disease. Prevalence estimates place Alzheimer’s at ~50% and vascular dementia at ~20%.

questions.question_text: Antipsychotics have been known to have an effect on the corrected QT (QTC) interval. Which of the following antidepressants would also have an effect on the QTC interval?
questions.explanation: Trazodone can prolong the QTc interval and may cause postural hypotension. Fluoxetine, paroxetine and sertraline have minimal effects on QTc.

questions.question_text: Based on previous research, the estimated incidence of a child developing schizophrenia if one parent has been affected has been estimated to be
questions.explanation: The risk to offspring if one parent is affected is about 13%. If both parents are affected, the risk rises to approximately 46%.

questions.question_text: The tract that connects the Wernicke’s and the Broca’s area is commonly referred to as the arcuate fasciculus. Lesions involving this particular tract would lead to which one of the following?
questions.explanation: Damage to the arcuate fasciculus produces conduction aphasia: fluent spontaneous speech and good comprehension but an inability to repeat phrases, plus phonemic paraphasias.

questions.question_text: A forensic psychiatrist was giving a lecture to medical students and asked them to guess the estimated prevalence of antisocial personality disorder amongst the general population in the United Kingdom. The correct answer should be
questions.explanation: Community prevalence of antisocial personality disorder is estimated at around 0.6%–3.0%, with a higher rate in males (approximately 6:1 male:female ratio).

questions.question_text: An 18-year-old male was involved in a road traffic accident nearly 3 months ago. Currently, he has symptoms of avoidance, hyper-arousal and emotional numbing. Which of the following psychotherapies would be suitable to help him with his condition?
questions.explanation: NICE guidelines recommend trauma-focused CBT within 3 months of PTSD symptoms, with 8–12 sessions focusing on trauma processing, exposure and cognitive restructuring.

questions.question_text: It is not uncommon for adolescents to have suicidal ideations. What has been the estimated proportion of them having suicidal ideations over the past 1 year?
questions.explanation: Epidemiological surveys estimate that around 10% of adolescents report suicidal ideation during a one-year period.

questions.question_text: Post-mortem examination of the brains of those who have died from Wernicke’s encephalopathy revealed that there have been petechial haemorrhages in all of the following structures except?
questions.explanation: Wernicke’s encephalopathy is a medical emergency treated with IV thiamine. Post-mortem, petechial haemorrhages are found in mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey, inferior colliculi and walls of the third ventricle, but not in the walls of the lateral ventricle.

questions.question_text: Roughly what percentage of patients with Wernicke’s encephalopathy would have the classical triad of ataxia, ophthalmoplegia and memory disturbances?
questions.explanation: Although the classic triad occurs in teaching descriptions, only about 10% of patients actually present with all three of ataxia, ophthalmoplegia and confusion/memory disturbance.

questions.question_text: Chlorpromazine is known to be one of the first antipsychotics discovered. It is known to be an effective antiemetic as well. This is mainly due to its action on which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation: Chlorpromazine’s antiemetic effect is largely due to central D2 receptor blockade in the chemoreceptor trigger zone. All effective antipsychotics occupy a high proportion of D2 receptors.

questions.question_text: It is known that the stimulation of the opioid receptors would produce all of the following effects, with the exception of?
questions.explanation: Opioid receptor stimulation (especially μ-receptor) produces analgesia, euphoria, miosis, hypotension, bradycardia and respiratory depression. Hypertension is not a typical opioid effect.

questions.question_text: Which of the following opiate receptors is responsible for the development of opioid dependence?
questions.explanation: The μ-opioid receptor mediates the major rewarding and dependence-producing effects of opioids. Activation leads to inhibition of GABA release and increased dopamine in the nucleus accumbens.

questions.question_text: Which of the following structures is part of the brain’s reward pathway that has been implicated in addictive behaviours?
questions.explanation: The ventral tegmental area (VTA) contains dopaminergic neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex, forming the mesolimbic reward pathway implicated in addiction.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old male, Simon, has been referred by his nursing home doctor to the old-age psychiatrist for restlessness during sleep. The psychiatrist feels that Simon has signs and symptoms of REM sleep disorder. Which of the following medications would help in his signs and symptoms?
questions.explanation: REM sleep behaviour disorder responds well to low-dose clonazepam. It reduces muscle activity that causes acting out dreams.

questions.question_text: A core trainee is new to forensic psychiatry. He understands from his consultant that a patient was scheduled for a personality testing. He wonders which one of the following psychometric instruments would be able to assess the patient across at least nine different psychopathological domains. The correct answer would be
questions.explanation: The MMPI has over 550 items and yields scores on multiple clinical, validity and supplementary scales, covering a broad range of psychopathological domains.

questions.question_text: With regards to the epidemiology of substance misuse in the United Kingdom, which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.text: The peak age of substance misuse is 15 years old.
The male-to-female ratio for substance misuse has been estimated to be 3:1.
Fifty percent of the adolescents and young adults in the United Kingdom have taken illicit drugs at some point in time.
Twenty percent of them have used illicit substances in the previous month.
Five percent of them have used at least a minimum of two substances in the past one month.

correct_answer.text: The peak age of substance misuse is 15 years old.

correct_answers.text: The peak age of substance misuse is 15 years old.

questions.explanation: Nationwide surveys indicate the peak age for substance misuse is around 20 years, not 15.

questions.question_text: Astrocytes are present in the central nervous system (CNS). They are known to be multipolar and their functions involve all the following except:

options.text: Formation of the CNS neuroglial scar tissue

questions.explanation: Astrocytes contribute to the BBB, provide structural support, form glial scars and partake in phagocytosis, but they are not primarily neuromodulators.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the main pathological change in patients who have multiple sclerosis?
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by immune-mediated demyelination of CNS axons.

questions.question_text: A 38-year-old female has been diagnosed with moderate depression and the consultant psychiatrist is recommending to her antidepressant treatment. She is not keen about antidepressants, as she feels that they would lead to weight gain. Which of the following antidepressants is likely to cause the maximum weight gain?
questions.explanation: Doxepin, a tricyclic antidepressant with strong H1-histamine receptor antagonism, is associated with marked weight gain and sedation.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old was involved in a road traffic accident around 3 hours ago. He did not sustain any obvious injuries, but now he is complaining that he is having the worst headache of his life. Which of the following would be the most appropriate immediate investigation?
questions.explanation: Noncontrast CT is the first-line acute investigation for sudden severe headache to exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracranial hemorrhage or other space-occupying lesions. It detects intracranial shifts, bleeding, edema and mass lesions rapidly.

questions.question_text: A core trainee was taking his MRCPsych CASC examination. He noted that on examination, the patient was not able to perform the Luria’s hand sequence and also the Go–No–Go Test. Which area of the cerebral cortex is most likely to be implicated given the changes observed?
questions.explanation: An impaired performance on the Luria’s hand performance test implies a lesion involving most likely the frontal lobe. The left frontal lobe is involved in controlling language-related movement (Broca’s area), and the right frontal lobe is involved in the non-verbal abilities. Left frontal lobe damage leads to non-fluent speech (excessive dysphasia) and depression.

questions.question_text: Zolpidem is one of the hypnotics that have a relatively short half-life. Its main mechanism of action is on which of the following receptors?

options.text: Alpha subunit of the GABA receptor
Beta subunit of the GABA receptor
Gamma subunit of the GABA receptor
Omega 1 subunit of the GABA receptor
Omega 2 subunit of the GABA receptor

correct_answer.text: Omega 1 subunit of the GABA receptor

correct_answers.text: Omega 1 subunit of the GABA receptor

questions.explanation: The proposed mechanism of action of benzodiazepine is binding to the GABA(A) receptors, and in particular, the omega 1 subunit of the GABA receptor.

questions.question_text: There are various neuronal mechanisms regulating the intake of food. Which of the following is a gut hormone that is released to help in the regulation of intake?
questions.explanation: This is a neuropeptide that is released from the small intestine and helps in the regulation of the postprandial release of bile locally in the gut itself and to control the appetite in the central nervous system. CCKa receptors are involved in appetite and feeding, whereas CCKb receptors are involved in emotional behaviour.

questions.question_text: Corticotropin release factor (CRF) regulates the release of adrenocorticotropic hormone from the anterior pituitary. Which of the following statements about the clinical relevance of this neuropeptide is incorrect?

options.text: CRF concentration is elevated in patients who are depressed.
With antidepressant treatment, there would be an expected reduction in the CRF level in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of depressed patients.
There would be an increase in the ACTH release in depressed patients who are being challenged with CRF.
CRH overactivity has a correlation with panic attacks.
CRH overactivity has a correlation with alcohol withdrawal.

correct_answer.text: There would be an increase in the ACTH release in depressed patients who are being challenged with CRF.

correct_answers.text: There would be an increase in the ACTH release in depressed patients who are being challenged with CRF.

questions.explanation: It has been noted that injections of CRH would lead to depressive symptoms such as reduction in appetite, sex drive, weight loss and altered circadian rhythms. A blunted ACTH response is noted to CRF challenge in depressed patients.

questions.question_text: Alcohol is metabolized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Ethanol is acted upon by alcohol dehydrogenase, whose gene is on chromosome 4, and is converted into acetaldehyde, which is then further acted upon by aldehyde dehydrogenase and converted into acetate. The gene that codes for the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase is located on chromosome 4, whilst the gene for aldehyde dehydrogenase is located on chromosome 12.

questions.question_text: At which of the following ages would an infant display or show the characteristic stranger anxiety syndrome?
questions.explanation: This refers to what is commonly known as stranger anxiety. Fear of strangers is usually shown by infants between the age of 8 months and 1 year. It is not necessarily part of the attachment behaviour and may occur independent of separation anxiety.

questions.question_text: This refers to the proportion of a defined population that has or has had a given disease (at any time during each individual’s lifetime thus far) at a given point in time. Which terminology is correct?
questions.explanation: The lifetime prevalence refers to the proportion of a defined population that has or has had a given disease (at any time during each individual’s lifetime thus far) at a given point in time.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is known to be the smallest brain peptide?
questions.explanation: Thyrotropin-releasing factor is known to be the smallest brain peptide and has the ability to also reverse sedation caused by drugs due to the release of dopamine and acetylcholine in the brain.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications acts as a partial agonist at a receptor site?
questions.explanation: The aforementioned drug is considered to be a partial mu-opioid agonist and a partial k-opioid antagonist. The peak plasma concentration of the drug is observed approximately 3 hours after dose administration. It has a terminal half-life of about 3–5 hours. The primary side effects of the medication include nausea, vomiting and constipation. The side effects may be less intense than those produced by the full opioid agonist opioids.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the correct terminology describing a structure whose ultrastructure consists of protein neurofilaments, granular materials, dense core vesicles, microtubule assembly protein, ubiquitin and tau protein?
questions.explanation: The aforementioned description correlates to the ultra-structural pathology of Lewy bodies.

questions.question_text: These are cells that are present in the nervous system, which aid in the flow of the CSF. Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: These are cells that line the cavities of the CNS and their function is to aid in the flow of the CSF through cilial beating.

questions.question_text: Juvenile delinquency is defined as a law-breaking behaviour engaged by those who are between 10 and 21 years old. The factors associated with juvenile delinquency include all of the following, with the exception of
questions.explanation: All of the aforementioned are associated factors, with the exception of small family size. A large family size has been implicated.

questions.question_text: Based on the social class classification system, a 17-year-old female, Alice, and her family belong to the lower social class. As compared to the upper social class, which one of the following psychiatric conditions would Alice be less susceptible to acquire?
questions.explanation: Eating disorders such as anorexia have a higher prevalence in higher socioeconomic classes and Western Caucasians and a significant association with greater parental education.

questions.question_text: It has been known that clozapine has the highest affinity for which of the following dopamine receptors?
questions.explanation: Clozapine is almost 20–25 times more potent at the D4 receptors than the D2 receptors.

questions.question_text: Somatostatin is a neuropeptide that has an inhibitory effect on growth hormone release. A decrease in its concentration in the CSF is expected for patients with which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: The CSF concentration is decreased in unipolar and bipolar depression as well as in Alzheimer’s disease.

questions.question_text: Based on epidemiology studies, what percentage of dementia in the general population is due to vascular causes?
questions.explanation: The estimated percentage of vascular dementia amongst the general population has been estimated to be around 15%.

questions.question_text: Based on the World Health Organization classification system, which one of the following terminologies correctly describes the number of stillbirths and deaths in the first week of life per 1000 live births?
questions.explanation: Perinatal mortality rate refers to the number of stillbirths and deaths in the first week of life per 1000 live births.

questions.question_text: Who was responsible for proposing a dimensional rather than a categorical approach to the description of personality?
questions.explanation: In 1978, Eysenck proposed a dimensional rather than a categorical approach to the description of personality.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications would be the most appropriate for patients who need minimal night sedation, without hangover effects the next day?
questions.explanation: Zolpidem has the shortest half-life when administered. It is believed to achieve a central hypnotic effect by acting on the same receptors as do benzodiazepines.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not one of the structures of the peripheral nervous system?

options.text: Cell bodies lying outside the CNS

questions.explanation: The dura, arachnoid and pia mater are part of the meninges and not part of the peripheral nervous system. All other structures listed belong to the PNS.

questions.question_text: Which of the following defence mechanisms is considered to be a mature defence mechanism?
questions.explanation: Sublimation is a mature defence mechanism and it involves a process that utilizes the force of a sexual instinct in drives, affects and memories in order to motivate creative activities having no apparent connection to the sexual instincts.

questions.question_text: All of the following medications would have an interaction with the mood stabilizer lithium, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Lithium interacts with NSAIDs (diclofenac, ibuprofen) and diuretics (frusemide, thiazides) but does not have a significant interaction with fluoxetine.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old female has always been afraid of heights. She is increasingly finding it difficult to get to work, as her new workplace is on the twentieth floor in central London. Which of the following psychological therapies would be best indicated for her?
questions.explanation: Desensitization therapy is a behavioural technique introduced by Wolpe, combining relaxation with graded exposure to the feared stimulus.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements with regards to mortality statistics is incorrect?

options.text: The mortality rate refers to the number of deaths in a defined population during a given period of time divided by the population size during that period.
The mortality rate is sometimes also referred to as the crude mortality rate.
The standardized mortality rate is the mortality rate that has been adjusted to compensate for a potential confounder.
The age-standardized mortality rate is the mortality rate that has been adjusted to compensate for the confounding effect of age.
The standardized mortality ratio is obtained from the standardized mortality rate multiplied by 100.

correct_answer.text: The standardized mortality ratio is obtained from the standardized mortality rate multiplied by 100.

correct_answers.text: The standardized mortality ratio is obtained from the standardized mortality rate multiplied by 100.

questions.explanation: The standardized mortality ratio is actually the ratio of the observed standardized mortality rate derived from the population being studied to the expected standardized mortality rate derived from a comparable standard population.

questions.question_text: Thomas and Chess previously described several different kinds of temperaments. Which of the following is not described by them?
questions.explanation: Option (d) Avoidant is incorrect. They proposed three temperament types: the easy child, the difficult child and the slow-to-warm-up child.

questions.question_text: Amongst the following options, which is the commonest defence mechanism used by patients with borderline personality disorder?
questions.explanation: Splitting refers to segregating good objects, affects and memories from bad ones. It is the hallmark defence mechanism in borderline personality disorder.

questions.question_text: A medical student is curious as to which of the following antipsychotics has the same structure and belongs to the same family as paliperidone. The correct answer would be
questions.explanation: Paliperidone is a derivative of risperidone. For risperidone, it has a higher risk for extrapyramidal side effects and galactorrhoea compared to other second-generation antipsychotics. Paliperidone shares the same chemical structure.

questions.question_text: A medical student attached to the Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS) service was keen to know the estimated prevalence of psychiatric disorders in adolescence. The correct answer would be
questions.explanation: Epidemiological studies estimate the prevalence of psychiatric disorders in adolescence at around 10%–20%, with a male-to-female ratio of approximately 1:1.5.

questions.question_text: This refers to the proportion of a defined population that has a given disease during a given interval of time. Which terminology is correct?
questions.explanation: Period prevalence refers to the proportion of a defined population that has a given disease during a specified interval of time.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements with regards to the measures of incidence is incorrect?

options.text: The alternative name for incidence is that of incidence rate.
The alternative name for cumulative incidence is that of risk.
Incidence refers to the number of new events during a specified period.
Cumulative incidence refers to the proportion of a population who develops the disease of interest in a defined period.
Incidence is affected by the disease survival.

correct_answer.text: Incidence is affected by the disease survival.

correct_answers.text: Incidence is affected by the disease survival.

questions.explanation: Incidence is not affected by the disease survival. The denominator usually includes those who are at risk.

questions.question_text: The interaction between lamotrigine and which of the following medications would cause a marked increase in the serum levels of lamotrigine?
questions.explanation: Sodium valproate works by increasing the amount of GABA, decreasing the GABA breakdown, increasing the GABA release and decreasing the turnover of GABA. Lamotrigine works by the inhibition of glutamate release. Interaction between lamotrigine and sodium valproate causes a marked increase in the levels of lamotrigine.

questions.question_text: As compared to the normal population, what is the increase in the risk of acquiring schizophrenia for a monozygotic twin?
questions.explanation: Based on prior studies, the concordance rate for monozygotic twins has been approximately 45%, whereas that for dizygotic twins has been approximately 10%.

questions.question_text: Based on epidemiological studies, what has been estimated to be the 1-year prevalence of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: The estimated 1-year prevalence of schizophrenia has been estimated to be around 1%.

questions.question_text: The lifetime risk of adults in the general population suffering from bipolar disorder has been estimated to be around
questions.explanation: The lifetime risk for adults in the general population that has bipolar disorder has been estimated to be around 1%.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the epidemiology of depressive disorder is incorrect?

options.text: The prevalence in the general population has been estimated to be around 2%–5%.
The peak age of onset of the first episode of depression has been estimated to be around 30 years old.
Social factors that contribute to depressive disorder include unemployment, separation and divorce.
The first major depressive episode in old people is often associated with an undiagnosed neurological disorder.

questions.explanation: The female-to-male ratio is actually around 2:1, not 1:2.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old male has been advised by his colleagues to seek help from his local GP. His colleagues have noted that he has been more irritable at work recently. He shares that he is having some marital relationship issues with his wife. Which of the following defence mechanisms is in play?
questions.explanation: The defence mechanism in play is displacement. In displacement, emotions, ideas or wishes are transferred from their original object to a more acceptable substitute.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about polyploidy is correct?

options.text: It refers to the presence of 3n number of chromosomes.
It refers to the presence of 4n number of chromosomes.
It refers to the presence of multiple sets of chromosomes.
It refers to the replicated nuclear material prior to cellular replication and duplication.
It refers to the presence of multiple mutations within a set of chromosomes.

correct_answer.text: It refers to the presence of multiple sets of chromosomes.

correct_answers.text: It refers to the presence of multiple sets of chromosomes.

questions.explanation: Option (c) is correct, as it refers to the presence of multiple sets of chromosomes.

questions.question_text: The cerebellum is derived from which of the following primitive brain structures?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum is derived from the metencephalon. Other derivatives include the pons and also part of the medulla oblongata.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the epidemiology of schizophrenia is incorrect?

options.text: The lifetime prevalence of the disorder has been estimated to be around 1.4%.
There is an unequal gender ratio, with males being more affected than females.
The mean age of onset for men is between 15 and 25 years.
The mean age of onset for women is between 25 and 35 years.
The association between schizophrenia and low social class is seen as a consequence rather than an aetiology of schizophrenia.

correct_answer.text: There is an unequal gender ratio, with males being more affected than females.

correct_answers.text: There is an unequal gender ratio, with males being more affected than females.

questions.explanation: Schizophrenia has an equal lifetime prevalence in males and females, although men tend to have earlier onset.

questions.question_text: Which of the following chromosomal types is characterized by the presence of a centromere at the tail?
questions.explanation: Acrocentric refers to a chromosome in which the centromere is very near to one end.

questions.question_text: A medical student attending the neurology class has been having difficulties with understanding and comprehending the concepts in neurology. He wonders which of the following is not considered a type of neuroglia in the CNS. The correct answer would be
questions.explanation: Neuroglia in the CNS include astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and ependymal cells. Satellite cells are part of the peripheral nervous system.

questions.question_text: The main functions of astrocytes include all of the following, with the exception of

options.text: They help in the support of neurons.
They are actively involved in phagocytosis.
They are responsible for forming the CNS neuroglial scar tissue.
They are responsible for immune control.
They help to contribute to the blood–brain barrier.

correct_answer.text: They are responsible for immune control.

correct_answers.text: They are responsible for immune control.

questions.explanation: There are typically two main types of astrocytes: the fibrous and the protoplasmic astrocytes. They are responsible for all the aforementioned, with the exception of immune mediation. Astrocytes are considered to be multi-polar.

questions.question_text: What are the chances of children acquiring an autosomal recessive disorder, in situations in which both parents carry one abnormal copy of the gene?
questions.explanation: When both parents carry one abnormal copy of the gene, there is a 25% chance of a child inheriting both mutations, hence expressing the disorder.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old female is about to enter university. She has come for an assessment at the university health centre, as she is concerned about her chances of acquiring bipolar disorder, given that her sister has it. The chances of her acquiring the disorder would be
questions.explanation: The lifetime risk for first-degree relatives has been estimated to be around 4%–18%.

questions.question_text: A lesion involving which of the following would lead to expressive motor aphasia?

options.text: Frontal operculum on the dominant side
Frontal operculum on the non-dominant side

correct_answer.text: Frontal operculum on the dominant side

correct_answers.text: Frontal operculum on the dominant side

questions.explanation: Expressive (Broca’s) aphasia results from a lesion in the frontal operculum on the dominant side, involving Brodmann areas 44 and 45.

questions.question_text: Prior research has demonstrated that a lesion involving this area could potentially lead to a form of acquired sociopathy. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Frontal operculum on the dominant side
Frontal operculum on the non-dominant side

questions.explanation: Lesions involving the orbital cortex on either side have been shown to lead to a form of acquired sociopathy.

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist started a patient on a new antidepressant and he presented back to the clinic with swollen eyes and lips. Which type of adverse drug reaction would this be classified as?
questions.explanation: This presentation of angioedema (swollen eyes and lips) is IgE-mediated and thus classified as a Type I hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.question_text: A lesion involving which of the following structures would lead to akinetic mutism?

options.text: Frontal operculum on the dominant side
Frontal operculum on the non-dominant side

questions.explanation: Lesions involving the superior mesial region (supplementary motor area and anterior cingulate cortex) can lead to akinetic mutism.

questions.question_text: What is the prevalence of dysthymia in the general population based on epidemiological studies?
questions.explanation: The average prevalence of dysthymia in the general population has been estimated to be around 5%.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old male who has been an inpatient for the past 3 months has been recently commenced on clozapine for his treatment-resistant schizophrenia. The consultant psychiatrist in charge of his case was alerted by the lab, as he has developed neutropenia. Which type of adverse drug reaction would neutropenia be classified under?
questions.explanation: Neutropenia as a drug-induced cytotoxic effect is classified as a Type II hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.question_text: Haloperidol is classified as a typical antipsychotic. Based on the structure of haloperidol, which family or class of antipsychotics would it belong to?
questions.explanation: Haloperidol belongs to the butyrophene class of typical antipsychotics.

questions.question_text: Studies have shown that there is less than the normal number of chromosomes in some genetic disorders. Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Turner’s syndrome is characterized by monosomy X (45,X), resulting in fewer than the normal complement of chromosomes.

questions.question_text: Which of the following techniques can be used to detect trinucleotide repeat expansion?
questions.explanation: Southern blotting can detect large triplet repeat expansions better than PCR can, and is used for diagnosing disorders such as fragile X syndrome.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antipsychotics and its related antipsychotic class is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Clozapine is correctly classified as a dibenzodiazepine.

questions.question_text: A core trainee has been asked to review one of the patients in the gastroenterology ward. The patient was noted to have alcohol withdrawal syndrome. The most recent investigation showed that his liver function test was abnormal. Which one of the following medications would be the most appropriate?
questions.explanation: In patients with hepatic impairment, shorter-acting benzodiazepines such as oxazepam are preferred for treating alcohol withdrawal.

questions.question_text: Chlorpromazine has been known to be one of the first antipsychotics discovered. It belongs to the class of phenothiazines, but differs from the rest of the members of the same class as it has
questions.explanation: Chlorpromazine differs from other phenothiazines by having an aliphatic side chain.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding discontinuation of antidepressants is incorrect?

options.text: It would be wise to gradually reduce the dose of antidepressants over a period of 4 weeks.
For antidepressants that have a shorter half-life, a shorter period is required for discontinuation.
For antidepressants that have a longer half-life, a shorter period is required for discontinuation.
If the patient experiences unpleasant discontinuation symptoms, it would be wise to consider reintroduction of the original antidepressant at the dose that was effective.
Fluoxetine is a medication with a long half-life, whereas paroxetine is a medication with a short half-life.

correct_answer.text: For antidepressants that have a shorter half-life, a shorter period is required for discontinuation.

correct_answers.text: For antidepressants that have a shorter half-life, a shorter period is required for discontinuation.

questions.explanation: Longer taper periods are required for antidepressants with shorter half-lives (e.g., paroxetine, venlafaxine). Discontinuation should be gradual over at least 4 weeks. If unpleasant symptoms occur, reintroduce the effective dose. Fluoxetine has a long half-life, paroxetine a short half-life.

questions.question_text: A medical student wonders which one of the following would not be caused by a lesion involving the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. The correct answer would be
questions.explanation: All of the aforementioned, with the exception of sociopathy, are changes related to lesions involving the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. In addition, there would be poor organization, planning, abstraction and disturbances in motor programming.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements pertaining to epidemiological findings with regards to schizoaffective disorder is incorrect?

options.text: The incidence is not known, but it is known to be relatively less common than schizophrenia.
The prevalence is usually less than 1%.
It affects women more than men.
The age of onset is earlier for women compared with men.
The depressive subtype of schizoaffective disorder is more common in elders than in young persons.

correct_answer.text: The age of onset is earlier for women compared with men.

correct_answers.text: The age of onset is earlier for women compared with men.

questions.explanation: The age of onset is actually later in women compared with men.

questions.question_text: Which of the following theorists suggested the ‘split mind’ of schizophrenia and influenced Bleuler to develop a theory of fragmentation of mental activities in schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Both Freud and Bleuler believed in the ‘split mind’ or fragmentation of mental activities in schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements with regards to the gender differences in people with schizophrenia is false?

options.text: Men have bimodal peak of incidence.

correct_answer.text: Men have bimodal peak of incidence.

correct_answers.text: Men have bimodal peak of incidence.

questions.explanation: The incidence of schizophrenia is between 15 and 30 new cases per 100 000 per year, with a single early peak in men (15–25 years) and a bimodal peak in women (late 20s and around 50 years).

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old motorcyclist suffers from head injuries after a road traffic accident. His partner comments that his memory has become very poor. Which of the following is not a standardized test to assess his memory?
questions.explanation:
WCFST is a test mainly for executive function. AVLT is a 15-item 
five-trial test, from which recall (immediate and delayed) and recognition memory 
can be assessed. CVLT involves a list of 16 words. The list is repeated five times. 
Then, a second list is given, serving to interfere with the first list, after which recall 
of the first list is requested. RMT involves recognition of non-verbal material with 
interference from distracters after the first initial image is presented. The WMT 
assesses several memory components including concentration and summary indices that can be derived with a mean of 100. Tasks under WMT include 
assessment of logical memory (subjects are asked to recall the content of two stores 
read to them with a 30-minute delay) and a verbal paired associates test (learning 
word pairs, e.g. baby cries, and recalling the second word when the first word is 
given)

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms of schizophrenia is not a first-rank symptom?
questions.explanation: First-rank symptoms include audible thoughts, delusional perception, thought insertion and voices discussing or arguing. Formal thought disorder is not a first-rank symptom.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman was admitted to the ward and the nurses are having difficulty with her. She appears to be arrogant, refuses to follow ward rules and insists to drink alcohol in the ward. She believes that she is a ‘special’ patient and requests first-class treatment. Her husband mentions that she tends to exploit others and most people try to avoid her. Which defence mechanism is most often used by people with such disorder?
questions.explanation:
his person suffers from narcissistic personality disorder. 
Rationalization is the defence mechanism most commonly used by people with 
narcissistic personality disorder.

questions.question_text: You are the specialist trainee on the inpatient psychiatric ward. A patient with schizophrenia is admitted to the ward. He complains of having tremor and rigidity after taking haloperidol. The specialist trainee has consulted you on the appropriate scale to assess the potential side effects of antipsychotics. Which of the following scales would you recommend?
questions.explanation: The Simpson–Angus Scale is used to rate extrapyramidal side‐effects such as rigidity, tremor and akinesia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following movement disorders is not typically associated with schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Mannerisms are stereotyped purposeless movements more characteristic of catatonia, whereas ambitendency, mitgehen/mitmachen, negativism and stupor can be seen in schizophrenic catatonic features.

questions.question_text: The copying of a genetic message from mRNA to protein via tRNA is known as
questions.explanation: Translation is the process whereby mRNA is used as a template and tRNA brings amino acids to form a growing polypeptide chain.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding molecular genetics is false?

options.text: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) can detect small changes caused by mutations.
PCR requires large amounts of DNA.
Southern blotting can detect large triplet repeat expansions better than PCR can.
Northern blotting involves the analysis of RNA.
In expression microarray, mRNA from the tissue is converted into cDNA using reverse transcriptase and the cDNA is then labelled using different-coloured fluorochromes.

correct_answer.text: PCR requires large amounts of DNA.

correct_answers.text: PCR requires large amounts of DNA.

questions.explanation: PCR amplifies minute quantities of DNA and does not require large starting amounts.

questions.question_text: What is the increased risk for developing Alzheimer’s disease in an individual with ε2/ε4 alleles for the ApoE4 gene compared with the general population?
questions.explanation: Individuals with ε2/ε4 genotype have a three- to fourfold increased risk compared with the general population. Homozygous ε4/ε4 have about a tenfold increase.

questions.question_text: Which of the following diseases has an autosomal dominant form in a proportion of cases?
questions.explanation: Parkinson’s disease can have autosomal dominant familial forms, such as those due to alpha-synuclein gene mutations.

questions.question_text: Mutations in all of the following genes are associated with the development of schizophrenia, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Genes implicated in schizophrenia include DRD3 (D3 receptor), 5-HT2A, dysbindin (DTNBP1) and neuregulin. EPN2 is not associated.

questions.question_text: Genetic knockout mice lacking the gene for which of the following neuropeptides have been reported to exhibit narcolepsy?
questions.explanation: Orexin (hypocretin) knockout mice exhibit narcolepsy; human narcolepsy is associated with loss of hypothalamic orexin neurons.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding trisomy and non-disjunction of chromosome 21 is false?

options.text: Non-disjunction involves failure of a pair of chromosomes to separate normally during one of the meiotic divisions.
In 50% of Down syndrome cases, the non-disjunction event occurs during anaphase in maternal meiosis.
If non-disjunction occurs during anaphase in maternal meiosis, the result is two maternal copies of chromosome 21 plus one paternal copy.
If non-disjunction occurs during maternal meiosis, then the foetus inherits two copies of one of its mother’s number 21 chromosomes.
Non-disjunction occurs more frequently in maternal meiosis owing to its longer duration compared with paternal meiosis.

correct_answer.text: In 50% of Down syndrome cases, the non-disjunction event occurs during anaphase in maternal meiosis.

correct_answers.text: In 50% of Down syndrome cases, the non-disjunction event occurs during anaphase in maternal meiosis.

questions.explanation: In approximately 95% of Down syndrome cases, non-disjunction occurs during maternal meiosis, not just 50%.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Klinefelter’s syndrome is false?

options.text: The incidence is approximately 1 in 1000 newborn boys.
Eighty percent of males with Klinefelter’s syndrome have a 47,XXY karyotype with the additional X chromosome being derived equally from meiotic errors in each parent.
Newborn boys with Klinefelter’s syndrome are clinically normal.
Fertility in Klinefelter’s syndrome is severely impaired, and risks to offspring are usually irrelevant.
Patients with Klinefelter’s syndrome usually have affected siblings.

correct_answer.text: Patients with Klinefelter’s syndrome usually have affected siblings.

correct_answers.text: Patients with Klinefelter’s syndrome usually have affected siblings.

questions.explanation: Klinefelter’s syndrome typically occurs sporadically; affected individuals rarely have similarly affected siblings.

questions.question_text: This usually occurs around 15–30 months of age.
questions.explanation: The anal phase spans roughly 15–30 months, when erotic pleasure centers on bowel control and excretion.

questions.question_text: This is the stage in which pleasure is derived mainly from sucking.
questions.explanation: The oral phase (birth to ~15 months) focuses on mouth activities such as sucking for gratification.

questions.question_text: This is the stage that occurs from around age 5–6 years to the onset of puberty.
questions.explanation: The latency phase (about 6 years to puberty) is marked by a relative calm in psychosexual development.

questions.question_text: This is the stage in life in which there is a strong resurgence in the sexual drive.
questions.explanation: The genital phase begins at puberty, with renewed sexual interests and mature sexual relationships.

questions.question_text: Males with this particular karyotype will show an increased rate of petty crime.
questions.explanation: Males with XYY karyotype have been found to have higher rates of impulsivity and petty criminal behavior.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old male has some learning disability and comes to seek help for fertility problems. Physical exam shows small testes. Which karyotype is most likely?
questions.explanation: 47XXY is Klinefelter’s syndrome, presenting with small firm testes, hypogonadism and infertility.

questions.question_text: Fetuses with this particular syndrome tend to develop hydrops fetalis due to delayed maturation of the lymphatic drainage system.
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome (45X) fetuses often develop hydrops fetalis from lymphatic dysplasia.

questions.question_text: This is an X-linked dominant disorder with low penetrance. Verbal IQ is usually better than performance IQ.
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is X-linked with CGG repeat expansions; affected males have moderate–severe intellectual disability with better verbal IQ.

questions.question_text: This is the most common cytogenetic cause of learning disability.
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 (Down’s syndrome) is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability.

questions.question_text: Patients with this disorder usually have a short stature, seizures (20% of patients), strabismus, mitral valve prolapse and single transverse palmar crease.
questions.explanation:
These are the characteristics clinical features of patients with 
fragile X syndrome. The tri-nucleotide repeats are found on the long arm of 
X chromosome.

questions.question_text: Patients with this disorder have short stature, low hairline, shield-shaped thorax, widely spaced nipples and coarctation of the aorta.
questions.explanation:
These are the characteristic clinical features of Turner’s syndrome. 
It is due to non-disjunction of the paternal XY that results in sex chromosomal 
abnormality.

questions.question_text: Newborn boys with this syndrome are clinically normal but may be passive in childhood and aggressive/antisocial after puberty.
questions.explanation:
The clinical features described refer Klinefelter’s syndrome. Fifty per 
cent are due to maternal and another 50% are due to paternal non-disjunction

questions.question_text: Patients with this syndrome usually have recurrent respiratory infections and die before age 10 years.
questions.explanation: Hurler’s syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis I) is autosomal recessive, with severe respiratory and cardiac involvement leading to early death.

questions.question_text: This gene is associated with the development of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
questions.explanation: DISC1 (Disrupted in Schizophrenia 1) has been implicated in both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder susceptibility.

questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs of chromosomes are responsible for the development of autism?
questions.explanation: Genetic loci on chromosomes 2q and 7q have been linked to autism spectrum disorders.

questions.question_text: This chromosome is involved in the regulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor and is also one of the chromosomes responsible for bipolar affective disorder.
questions.explanation: Chromosome 11p contains the BDNF gene and has been implicated in bipolar disorder.

questions.question_text: Which of the following chromosomes and genes are responsible for the development of Alzheimer’s disease?
questions.explanation: Mutations in presenilin 1 (PSEN1), presenilin 2 (PSEN2) and the APOE gene on chromosome 19 increase Alzheimer’s risk.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a chromosome that is implicated in Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD)?
questions.explanation: Mutations in the PRNP gene on chromosome 20 are linked to inherited forms of CJD.

questions.question_text: This particular pathology of the pupil is associated with diminished and absent knee jerk.
questions.explanation: Holmes–Adie pupil shows dilated pupil with poor light response and diminished/absent reflexes, especially knee jerks.

questions.question_text: This particular pathology of the eye is associated with rapidly raising unilateral intracranial pressure.
questions.explanation: Hutchinson’s pupil (blown pupil) results from oculomotor nerve compression in acute unilateral intracranial pressure rises.

questions.question_text: This particular pathology of the eye is due to an underlying neurosyphilis and diabetes mellitus.
questions.explanation: Argyll Robertson pupil is small, irregular, unreactive to light but constricts on accommodation, seen in neurosyphilis and diabetes.

questions.question_text: This particular pathology of the eye is due to an underlying brain stem stroke, Pancoast tumour at the lung apex or carotid dissection.
questions.explanation: Horner’s syndrome results from interruption of sympathetic pathways, as in brain stem stroke, lung apex tumour or carotid dissection.

questions.question_text: The common clinical features include preservation of the dorsal column function, but the loss of all other functions. Which spinal cord lesion is this?
questions.explanation: Anterior cord syndrome spares dorsal column function (proprioception, vibration) but impairs motor and spinothalamic pathways.

questions.question_text: The common clinical features include early sphincter disturbances, spinothalamic loss and loss of pain and temperature sensation. There is noted to be spasticity below the level of the lesions. Which spinal cord lesion is this?
questions.explanation: Central cord lesions often produce bilateral pain/temperature loss at the level, early bladder dysfunction and spasticity below due to lateral CST involvement.

questions.question_text: The common clinical features include ipsilateral spasticity and pyramidal signs. There might also be posterior column sensory loss and contralateral spinothalamic loss. Which spinal cord lesion is this?
questions.explanation: Brown–Séquard hemisection causes ipsilateral UMN signs and dorsal column loss, with contralateral pain/temperature loss a few segments below.

questions.question_text: In this condition, there is loss of all functions below the level of the lesion. Which spinal cord lesion is this?
questions.explanation: Total transection of the spinal cord produces complete loss of motor, sensory and autonomic function below the lesion.

questions.question_text: This is a descending anterior tract that is involved in motor functioning.
questions.explanation: The reticulospinal tract descends in the anterior funiculus and mediates posture and gross motor functions.

questions.question_text: This is a descending anterior tract that is involved in voluntary movement.
questions.explanation: The anterior corticospinal tract carries voluntary motor signals to axial musculature and travels in the anterior columns.

questions.question_text: This is a descending anterior tract that is involved in muscle tone control.
questions.explanation: The vestibulospinal tract descends in the anterior columns and regulates extensor muscle tone for balance and posture.

questions.question_text: This is a descending lateral tract involved in visceral function control.
questions.explanation: Descending autonomic fibers run in the lateral funiculus to regulate sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow.

questions.question_text: The individual usually presents with an abrupt onset of disorientation, loss of ability to encode recent memories and retrograde amnesia for variable duration. The patient, however, still has a remarkable degree of alertness and responsiveness. The episode usually lasts for a few hours and is never repeated.
questions.explanation: Transient global amnesia is sudden, transient inability to form new memories and patchy retrograde loss, with preserved alertness and recovery within hours.

questions.question_text: This involves confabulation, report of false events and false confessions.
questions.explanation: False memory syndrome refers to confident recollections of events that never occurred, often with confabulation and false confessions.

questions.question_text: This is defined as the memory loss from the time of accident to the time that the patient can give a clear account of the recent events.
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic amnesia is the interval following a head injury during which the patient cannot form continuous memories until clear recall returns.

questions.question_text: This refers to the inability to form new memories.
questions.explanation: Anterograde amnesia is the inability to encode and retain new information after the onset of amnesia.

questions.question_text: This refers to the loss of memory for events that occurred prior to an event or condition.
questions.explanation: Retrograde amnesia is the loss of pre-existing memories for events preceding an injury or insult.

questions.question_text: The typical macroscopic changes for this particular condition include cerebral atrophy, ventricular enlargement, perforation of the cavum septum pellucidum and thinning of the corpus callosum.
questions.explanation: Punch-drunk encephalopathy (chronic traumatic encephalopathy) shows cerebral atrophy, ventricular enlargement, septum pellucidum changes and corpus callosum thinning.

questions.question_text: The typical macroscopic changes for this particular condition include selective cerebellar atrophy, generalized cerebral atrophy and also ventricular enlargement.
questions.explanation: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease shows rapid neurodegeneration with selective cerebellar and generalized cerebral atrophy and ventricular enlargement in slower cases.

questions.question_text: The typical macroscopic changes for this particular condition include selective symmetrical atrophy of the anterior temporal lobes and the frontal lobes, knife-blade gyri and ventricular enlargement.
questions.explanation: Pick’s disease (frontotemporal dementia) shows severe focal atrophy of frontal and temporal poles ('knife-blade' gyri) and ventricular dilation.

questions.question_text: The typical macroscopic changes for this particular condition include global brain atrophy and low brain mass, ventricular enlargement and sulcal widening.
questions.explanation: Alzheimer’s disease is characterized by diffuse cortical atrophy, widened sulci and enlarged ventricles.

questions.question_text: The main use of this form of imaging is for trauma assessment.
questions.explanation: Skull X-rays are largely replaced but historically used for acute head trauma screening to detect fractures and gross lesions.

questions.question_text: One of the main uses of this form of imaging is for neuropsychiatric research. It is able to pick up shifts of intracranial pressure and cerebral infarction.
questions.explanation: CT scanning provides rapid structural images to detect hemorrhage, infarction, edema, mass effect and midline shift.

questions.question_text: This particular form of imaging can give information about metabolic changes.
questions.explanation: PET imaging measures regional cerebral metabolism (e.g., FDG-PET) and neurotransmitter receptor binding.

questions.question_text: This particular form of imaging is of use in conditions in which the onset of symptoms is being studied.
questions.explanation: SPECT allows injection of radioligands at symptom onset and delayed imaging, useful in epilepsy or acute neuropsychiatric events.

questions.question_text: This is the preferred form of neuroanatomical imaging for clinical and research studies that require high-resolution neuroanatomical imaging.
questions.explanation: MRI provides superior soft-tissue contrast and high-resolution structural images without ionizing radiation.

questions.question_text: This term is also known as risk.
questions.explanation: Cumulative incidence (risk) is the proportion of a population developing a disease over a given period.

questions.question_text: This term is also known as incidence rate.
questions.explanation: Incidence (or incidence rate) is the number of new cases per population at risk per unit time.

questions.question_text: This term takes into account both the incidence and the chronicity.
questions.explanation: Point prevalence = Incidence × Duration (chronicity) in a stable population.

questions.question_text: This refers to the average duration of an illness condition.
questions.explanation: Chronicity (duration) is the average length of illness from onset to resolution or death.

questions.question_text: This terminology refers to the rate of occurrence of new cases of the disease in a defined population over a given period of time.
questions.explanation: Incidence is the count of new cases per population at risk during a time interval.

questions.question_text: This terminology refers to the proportion of a defined population that has disease at a given time.
questions.explanation: Point prevalence is the proportion of individuals in a population who have the disease at a specific point in time.

questions.question_text: This terminology is also otherwise known as the risk difference or absolute excess risk.
questions.explanation: Attributable risk (risk difference) is the incidence in exposed minus incidence in unexposed.

questions.question_text: This refers to the ratio of the odds that subjects in the disease group were exposed to the factor to the odds that subjects in the control group were exposed to the factor.
questions.explanation: Odds ratio is the odds of exposure among cases divided by odds of exposure among controls.

questions.question_text: This refers to the ratio of the incidence of the disease in people exposed to that risk factor to the incidence of the disease in people not exposed to the same risk factor.
questions.explanation: Relative risk = incidence in exposed ÷ incidence in unexposed.

questions.question_text: This refers to the mortality rate that is adjusted to compensate for a confounder.
questions.explanation: Standardized mortality rate is a mortality rate adjusted for confounding factors.

questions.question_text: This terminology refers to the ratio of the observed standardized mortality rate derived from the population being studied to the expected standardized mortality rate derived from a comparable standard population.
questions.explanation: Standardized mortality ratio = observed deaths ÷ expected deaths in a standard population.

questions.question_text: This terminology refers to the mean length of time that an individual can be expected to live based on the assumption that the mortality rates used remain constant.
questions.explanation: Life expectancy is the average number of years an individual is expected to live if current mortality rates persist.

questions.question_text: He denies being depressed and says that everything is fine. When the psychiatrist asks him how he feels about the amputation, he always evades the question and talks about something else.
questions.explanation: Denial is the refusal to accept reality or fact, avoiding awareness of painful aspects.

questions.question_text: He becomes angry with the psychiatrist for asking him questions about his work and family situation. He says that the psychiatrist deliberately makes his mood worse and there is nothing that can be done to help him.
questions.explanation: Projection attributes one’s own unacceptable feelings or intentions to another person.

questions.question_text: He is made to resign from work, as he cannot keep up to the demands of his job. He overhears colleagues saying sarcastic remarks about him. When he is at home, he scolds his wife badly for a trivial matter.
questions.explanation: Displacement redirects emotions from a ‘safer’ substitute target when direct expression is threatening.

questions.question_text: Two months later, after adequate pharmacological and psychotherapy treatment, he appears to be coping well and tells his psychiatrist that he has decided to help out in a volunteer social service catering to support the disabled.
questions.explanation: Sublimation channels unacceptable drives into socially acceptable and constructive activities.
